text: Tote bags need fabric that can support the intended load. Medium- to heavy-weight woven cotton, canvas, denim, or linen are common choices. Lightweight fabric may need a lining or reinforcement.
Use stable woven fabric for tote bodies and straps when possible. Stretch knits can distort under load; if using a knit, stabilize it and test the seams before construction.
Cut tote panels with their grainlines parallel to the fabric selvage unless the pattern specifies otherwise. Keeping the body and straps on grain helps reduce unwanted twisting and stretching.
Check the tote pattern for seam allowance. Add the stated allowance to each cut edge if pattern dimensions are finished measurements; do not add it twice if it is already included.

For printed tote fabric, place repeated or directional motifs consistently across the front and back panels. Matching a large motif can use extra fabric, so account for placement before deciding the scrap is large enough.
Lightweight or loosely woven tote fabric may benefit from fusible interfacing or a separate lining. Choose interfacing compatible with the fabric weight and test adhesion and drape on a small offcut.
Keep tote pattern pieces away from holes, stains that cannot be removed, thinning, severe fading, and frayed edges. Include damage-free seam allowance around the whole cut piece.

Woven cotton, linen, denim, and light canvas are suitable for many pouches. Lightweight fabric can work when lined or interfaced; heavier fabric may need a suitable needle and zipper installation method.
Stable woven fabric is usually easier to use around a pouch zipper. Stretch knits can ripple or stretch while sewing; stabilize zipper edges or choose a stretch-compatible construction.
Place pouch panels with the pattern grainline parallel to the selvage unless the pattern gives another direction. Check the direction of one-way prints so motifs are upright on the finished pouch.
Include the pattern's seam allowance when estimating pouch panel size. Leave room for zipper tabs, boxed corners, or gussets if those features are part of the design.

A lining can protect the inside of a pouch and cover interfacing. Lightweight outer fabric may need lightweight fusible interfacing; test it on an offcut to check for bubbles, stiffness, or color changes.
When pouch fabric has a prominent repeat or directional print, align the front and back motifs intentionally. Pattern matching may require extra fabric beyond the panel dimensions.
Do not place pouch panels, zipper edges, or seam allowances over holes, weak spots, permanent stains, or fraying. A damaged area can be cut out only if enough usable fabric remains for every piece.

Scrunchies can be made from woven cotton, lightweight linen, satin, or suitable knits. Slippery fabrics need careful handling; stretchy knits can be useful when their stretch and recovery suit the design.
A scrunchie is a small project, so a lightweight or medium-weight fabric strip is generally easier to gather around elastic than very heavy fabric. Thick fabric can make bulky seams and gathers.
For woven scrunchie fabric, cut the strip on grain for predictable behavior. A bias-cut strip has more give and can drape differently; use it only when that behavior is desired.
Check whether the scrunchie pattern dimensions include seam allowance. Small pieces still need enough allowance to enclose the elastic and turn the tube without cutting into the seam.
For a printed scrunchie, consider how much of the print will show after the strip is gathered. Large motifs may be obscured; small repeats or non-directional prints are easier to place.
Avoid holes, weak or thinning fabric, stains that cannot be removed, and frayed edges when cutting a scrunchie strip. Keep the full seam allowance in sound fabric.

Woven fabric is made from crossing lengthwise and crosswise yarns and usually stretches less along grain. Knits are looped and usually have more stretch. Identify the fabric structure before choosing a pattern and stitch.

Fabric weight affects drape, bulk, and sewing difficulty. Lightweight fabric suits small or gathered items; medium weight is versatile; heavy fabric can provide structure but may create bulky seams. Match the weight to the product and machine.

The grainline usually runs parallel to the selvage and lengthwise yarns. Place pattern grainline markings parallel to the selvage unless the pattern directs otherwise; off-grain pieces may twist or hang unevenly.

Seam allowance is the fabric between the stitching line and cut edge. Check each pattern's instructions because dimensions may be given as cut sizes or finished sizes; add the specified allowance only when it is not already included.

With a directional print, keep motifs upright and consistently oriented. With a repeat, match motifs at visible seams when practical. Matching prints can consume extra fabric, so include placement needs in the usable-size estimate.

Interfacing adds support or stability. Choose its weight and type to suit the fabric and pattern, and follow its application instructions. Test a small scrap first because heat or adhesive can change texture, color, or drape.

Inspect scraps before cutting. Avoid placing pattern pieces or seam allowances over holes, mold, contamination, severe thinning, permanent stains, or damaged edges. Measure only the continuous usable area that remains.
Before sewing unfamiliar fabric, test the needle, stitch length, tension, and seam finish on an offcut. Use a compatible needle and stitch for the fabric structure and thickness.
